q: A 22-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of bloody diarrhoea up to eight times daily, lower abdominal cramps and urgency. She has lost 4 kg. Examination shows mild left iliac fossa tenderness. Blood tests: haemoglobin 104 g/L, platelets 480 x10^9/L, CRP 62 mg/L, albumin 30 g/L. Stool cultures are negative and faecal calprotectin is 890 µg/g. Flexible sigmoidoscopy shows continuous erythematous, granular, friable mucosa extending from the rectum to the splenic flexure with no skip lesions. Biopsies show crypt abscesses and distorted crypt architecture confined to the mucosa. She is started on treatment and reviewed. Which single feature is most characteristic of the underlying diagnosis rather than the alternative inflammatory bowel disease?
options: Transmural inflammation on biopsy
Presence of non-caseating granulomas
Continuous mucosal inflammation extending proximally from the rectum
Perianal fistulating disease
Cobblestone appearance with skip lesions
explain: This is ulcerative colitis (UC). 🔬 The defining feature is continuous, confluent mucosal inflammation beginning at the rectum and extending proximally without skip lesions, confined to the mucosa and submucosa. Crypt abscesses and crypt architectural distortion support the diagnosis but also occur in Crohn's; continuity and rectal involvement are what distinguish UC. In contrast, transmural inflammation, non-caseating granulomas, perianal fistulae and a cobblestone/skip-lesion pattern are hallmarks of Crohn's disease, which can affect any part of the gut from mouth to anus. UC almost always involves the rectum and spreads contiguously. 📌 BSG guidance defines extent (proctitis, left-sided, extensive) which guides therapy — topical vs oral 5-ASA. This patient has left-sided moderately active UC; first-line induction is oral plus topical mesalazine, escalating to corticosteroids if inadequate.

Crypt abscesses and crypt architectural distortion support the diagnosis but also occur in Crohn's; continuity and rectal involvement are what distinguish UC. In contrast, transmural inflammation, non-caseating granulomas, perianal fistulae and a cobblestone/skip-lesion pattern are hallmarks of Crohn's disease, which can affect any part of the gut from mouth to anus. UC almost always involves the rectum and spreads contiguously. 📌 BSG guidance defines extent (proctitis, left-sided, extensive) which guides therapy — topical vs oral 5-ASA. This patient has left-sided moderately active UC; first-line induction is oral plus topical mesalazine, escalating to corticosteroids if inadequate.

A.html: Transmural inflammation extends through the full bowel wall and is a hallmark of Crohn's disease, predisposing to fistulae and strictures. UC inflammation is limited to the mucosa/submucosa, which is why perforation typically occurs only with toxic megacolon.

B.html: Non-caseating granulomas are found in up to 30% of Crohn's biopsies and are not a feature of UC. Their presence should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis.
B.text: Non-caseating granulomas are found in up to 30% of Crohn's biopsies and are not a feature of UC. Their presence should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis.

C.html: Correct. Continuous inflammation extending proximally from the rectum without skip areas is the defining macroscopic feature of UC, distinguishing it from the patchy, discontinuous distribution of Crohn's disease.
C.text: Correct. Continuous inflammation extending proximally from the rectum without skip areas is the defining macroscopic feature of UC, distinguishing it from the patchy, discontinuous distribution of Crohn's disease.

D.html: Perianal fistulating disease, skin tags and abscesses strongly favour Crohn's. Perianal complications are uncommon in UC and their presence argues against it.

E.html: A cobblestone mucosa with intervening normal skip lesions is classic of Crohn's. UC shows uniform, continuous granular friable mucosa without cobblestoning.
E.text: A cobblestone mucosa with intervening normal skip lesions is classic of Crohn's. UC shows uniform, continuous granular friable mucosa without cobblestoning.

q: A 34-year-old woman with a 10-year history of ulcerative colitis presents with a severe flare. She has 12 bloody stools daily, temperature 38.6°C, heart rate 118 bpm and abdominal distension. Blood tests: haemoglobin 92 g/L, white cells 18 x10^9/L, CRP 140 mg/L, albumin 24 g/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L. She is started on intravenous hydrocortisone. On day 2 her abdomen becomes markedly distended and tympanic with reduced bowel sounds. A supine abdominal radiograph shows transverse colon dilatation to 7 cm with mucosal islands. What is the most appropriate immediate management step?
options: Urgent surgical review for consideration of colectomy
Add oral mesalazine at maximum dose
Commence loperamide to reduce stool frequency
Perform full colonoscopy to assess disease extent
Arrange outpatient MRI enterography
explain: This is toxic megacolon complicating acute severe UC — a surgical emergency. 🚨 Diagnosis requires radiographic colonic dilatation (>5.5–6 cm transverse colon) plus systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia, leucocytosis, anaemia). This patient meets both. Management is joint medical–surgical: continue IV corticosteroids, aggressive fluid/electrolyte correction (correct the hypokalaemia — it worsens colonic atony), bowel rest, and urgent surgical review because of the high risk of perforation, which carries substantial mortality. If there is no improvement within 24–72 hours (or deterioration/perforation), subtotal colectomy is required. Antidiarrhoeals such as loperamide are contraindicated — they reduce motility and precipitate/worsen toxic megacolon. Colonoscopy is contraindicated due to perforation risk. Adding oral mesalazine does not treat acute severe colitis (steroids ± ciclosporin/infliximab as medical rescue do). Per BSG/ACPGBI, early surgical involvement and monitoring (stool chart, daily AXR, CRP) are essential; the Travis criteria on day 3 (>8 stools/day or CRP >45 with 3–8 stools) predict need for colectomy.

Per BSG/ACPGBI, early surgical involvement and monitoring (stool chart, daily AXR, CRP) are essential; the Travis criteria on day 3 (>8 stools/day or CRP >45 with 3–8 stools) predict need for colectomy.

A.html: Correct. Toxic megacolon mandates urgent surgical review with joint medical-surgical care. Failure to respond within 24–72 hours or any perforation requires subtotal colectomy; delay increases mortality.
A.text: Correct. Toxic megacolon mandates urgent surgical review with joint medical-surgical care. Failure to respond within 24–72 hours or any perforation requires subtotal colectomy; delay increases mortality.

B.html: Oral mesalazine has no role in inducing remission in acute severe colitis and does nothing for a dilated toxic colon. Medical rescue is with IV steroids then ciclosporin or infliximab, not 5-ASA.

C.html: Loperamide is contraindicated — antimotility and anticholinergic agents reduce colonic tone and can precipitate or worsen toxic megacolon and perforation.

D.html: Full colonoscopy is contraindicated in toxic megacolon and acute severe colitis because of the high risk of perforation. Limited flexible sigmoidoscopy with minimal insufflation may be used cautiously, but not full colonoscopy.

E.html: Outpatient MRI enterography is entirely inappropriate for an acutely toxic, potentially perforating colon requiring inpatient surgical assessment.

q: A 29-year-old woman presents with 6 months of bloating, intermittent diarrhoea, fatigue and a 5 kg weight loss. She reports an itchy vesicular rash over her elbows and knees. Blood tests show haemoglobin 101 g/L with a low mean corpuscular volume, ferritin 6 µg/L and folate at the lower limit of normal. Her GP requests coeliac serology while she remains on a normal gluten-containing diet. Which single test result, if positive, best supports the diagnosis and should prompt referral for confirmatory duodenal biopsy?
options: Anti-gliadin IgG antibodies
IgA tissue transglutaminase (tTG) antibodies with total IgA
HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping
Anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies (ASCA)
Faecal calprotectin
explain: The clinical picture — iron-deficiency anaemia, malabsorptive diarrhoea and an intensely itchy vesicular rash (dermatitis herpetiformis) — is classic coeliac disease. 🌾 NICE recommends first-line serology with IgA tissue transglutaminase (tTG), and total IgA must be measured simultaneously because selective IgA deficiency (10-fold commoner in coeliac) causes false-negative IgA tTG. If IgA is deficient, use IgG-based testing (IgG tTG or IgG endomysial antibody). Crucially, testing must be performed while the patient eats gluten (>6 weeks, gluten in >1 meal/day) or results are unreliable. A positive tTG mandates referral for duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis (Marsh classification) to confirm. Anti-gliadin antibodies are obsolete (poor sensitivity/specificity). HLA-DQ2/DQ8 has high negative predictive value (useful to exclude) but poor specificity as ~30% of the population carries these alleles, so it cannot confirm. ASCA relates to Crohn's; calprotectin is a non-specific inflammation marker.
explainHTML: The clinical picture — iron-deficiency anaemia, malabsorptive diarrhoea and an intensely itchy vesicular rash (dermatitis herpetiformis) — is classic coeliac disease. 🌾 NICE recommends first-line serology with IgA tissue transglutaminase (tTG), and total IgA must be measured simultaneously because selective IgA deficiency (10-fold commoner in coeliac) causes false-negative IgA tTG. If IgA is deficient, use IgG-based testing (IgG tTG or IgG endomysial antibody). Crucially, testing must be performed while the patient eats gluten (>6 weeks, gluten in >1 meal/day) or results are unreliable. A positive tTG mandates referral for duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis (Marsh classification) to confirm. Anti-gliadin antibodies are obsolete (poor sensitivity/specificity). HLA-DQ2/DQ8 has high negative predictive value (useful to exclude) but poor specificity as ~30% of the population carries these alleles, so it cannot confirm. ASCA relates to Crohn's; calprotectin is a non-specific inflammation marker.

A.html: Anti-gliadin antibodies have been superseded and are no longer recommended for coeliac screening because of poor sensitivity and specificity compared with tTG and endomysial antibodies.
A.text: Anti-gliadin antibodies have been superseded and are no longer recommended for coeliac screening because of poor sensitivity and specificity compared with tTG and endomysial antibodies.

B.html: Correct. IgA tTG with total IgA is the NICE first-line serological test. Measuring total IgA detects selective IgA deficiency, which would otherwise cause false-negative IgA tTG. A positive result warrants confirmatory duodenal biopsy.
B.text: Correct. IgA tTG with total IgA is the NICE first-line serological test. Measuring total IgA detects selective IgA deficiency, which would otherwise cause false-negative IgA tTG. A positive result warrants confirmatory duodenal biopsy.

C.html: HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing has excellent negative predictive value (a negative result virtually excludes coeliac) but poor specificity, as ~30% of the general population carry these alleles. It cannot confirm the diagnosis.
C.text: HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing has excellent negative predictive value (a negative result virtually excludes coeliac) but poor specificity, as ~30% of the general population carry these alleles. It cannot confirm the diagnosis.

D.html: ASCA positivity is associated with Crohn's disease, not coeliac disease, and has no role in this diagnostic pathway.
D.text: ASCA positivity is associated with Crohn's disease, not coeliac disease, and has no role in this diagnostic pathway.

E.html: Faecal calprotectin is a non-specific marker of intestinal inflammation useful in distinguishing IBD from IBS, but it neither diagnoses nor supports coeliac disease specifically.

q: A 58-year-old man with known alcohol-related cirrhosis and ascites presents with a 2-day history of abdominal pain, fever and worsening confusion. Observations: temperature 38.2°C, heart rate 104 bpm, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg. He has tense ascites and generalised abdominal tenderness. A diagnostic ascitic tap is performed. The ascitic fluid neutrophil (polymorphonuclear) count is 480 cells/mm³ and culture is pending. Serum bilirubin is 68 µmol/L, creatinine 96 µmol/L. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Intravenous cefotaxime and intravenous human albumin solution
Oral ciprofloxacin prophylaxis alone
Therapeutic large-volume paracentesis without antibiotics
Intravenous terlipressin and noradrenaline
Await ascitic culture results before starting antibiotics
explain: An ascitic neutrophil count ≥250 cells/mm³ is diagnostic of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), regardless of culture (which is often negative — 'culture-negative neutrocytic ascites'). Treatment must start immediately. 🦠 Pathogenesis is bacterial translocation from gut lumen, most commonly E. coli and other Gram-negatives. First-line therapy is an intravenous third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime) per EASL/BSG. Critically, giving intravenous albumin (1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3) reduces the incidence of hepatorenal syndrome and improves survival, particularly when bilirubin >68 µmol/L or creatinine >88 µmol/L — as here. Waiting for culture would dangerously delay treatment. Ciprofloxacin prophylaxis (secondary/primary) is for prevention after recovery, not acute treatment. Large-volume paracentesis without antibiotics ignores the infection. Terlipressin/noradrenaline treat established hepatorenal syndrome, not SBP itself. After an episode, patients should receive long-term oral norfloxacin/ciprofloxacin secondary prophylaxis.

After an episode, patients should receive long-term oral norfloxacin/ciprofloxacin secondary prophylaxis.

A.html: Correct. SBP (neutrophils ≥250/mm³) is treated with IV cefotaxime. Adding IV albumin reduces hepatorenal syndrome and improves survival, especially with bilirubin >68 µmol/L or raised creatinine, as in this patient.
A.text: Correct. SBP (neutrophils ≥250/mm³) is treated with IV cefotaxime. Adding IV albumin reduces hepatorenal syndrome and improves survival, especially with bilirubin >68 µmol/L or raised creatinine, as in this patient.

B.html: Oral ciprofloxacin is used for primary or secondary prophylaxis, not for treating an established episode of SBP, which requires prompt IV broad-spectrum antibiotics.
B.text: Oral ciprofloxacin is used for primary or secondary prophylaxis, not for treating an established episode of SBP, which requires prompt IV broad-spectrum antibiotics.

C.html: Draining ascites without antibiotics fails to treat the peritoneal infection. Large-volume paracentesis (with albumin cover) is a treatment for tense ascites, not SBP.
C.text: Draining ascites without antibiotics fails to treat the peritoneal infection. Large-volume paracentesis (with albumin cover) is a treatment for tense ascites, not SBP.

D.html: Terlipressin and noradrenaline are used to treat established hepatorenal syndrome or variceal bleeding, not the underlying infection of SBP. Antibiotics are the priority here.

E.html: SBP is frequently culture-negative, so treatment is guided by the neutrophil count and must not be delayed pending culture. Waiting risks progression to sepsis and death.

q: A 45-year-old man is admitted having taken an overdose of paracetamol 40 hours earlier as a single ingestion. He is jaundiced and drowsy. Investigations: INR 7.2, prothrombin time markedly prolonged, creatinine 340 µmol/L, arterial pH 7.24, lactate 4.2 mmol/L after adequate fluid resuscitation. He is disorientated in time and place (grade 2 encephalopathy). N-acetylcysteine is running. The hepatology and transplant teams are contacted. Which single feature most strongly indicates that he meets criteria for referral for emergency liver transplantation?
options: Serum bilirubin greater than 100 µmol/L
Peak ALT greater than 5000 U/L
Ingestion of more than 12 g of paracetamol
Arterial pH 7.24 after adequate fluid resuscitation
Isolated INR of 3.0 at 24 hours
explain: This is paracetamol-induced acute liver failure, and prognosis is assessed with the King's College Criteria. 🧪 For paracetamol, listing for emergency transplant is indicated if: • Arterial pH < 7.30 after adequate fluid resuscitation (regardless of encephalopathy grade), OR • All three of: INR > 6.5 (PT > 100s), creatinine > 300 µmol/L, AND grade 3–4 encephalopathy — within a 24-hour period. An arterial pH of 7.24 after resuscitation independently satisfies the criteria and is the single strongest indicator here. Lactate > 3.5 mmol/L after early resuscitation (or > 3.0 after full resuscitation) is an additional adverse marker. Bilirubin, ALT magnitude and the ingested dose do not feature in the paracetamol King's criteria. ALT correlates with hepatocyte necrosis but not outcome — the synthetic (INR) and metabolic (pH/lactate) derangements matter. His INR 7.2, creatinine 340 and grade 2 encephalopathy do not yet fulfil the combined criterion (needs grade 3–4), but the acidosis alone does. Continue NAC and involve a transplant centre urgently.

An arterial pH of 7.24 after resuscitation independently satisfies the criteria and is the single strongest indicator here. His INR 7.2, creatinine 340 and grade 2 encephalopathy do not yet fulfil the combined criterion (needs grade 3–4), but the acidosis alone does. Continue NAC and involve a transplant centre urgently.

A.html: Bilirubin is a component of the King's criteria for non-paracetamol acute liver failure but not the paracetamol criteria, which focus on pH, INR, creatinine and encephalopathy.
A.text: Bilirubin is a component of the King's criteria for non-paracetamol acute liver failure but not the paracetamol criteria, which focus on pH, INR, creatinine and encephalopathy.

B.html: Very high ALT reflects the extent of hepatocellular necrosis but does not predict outcome and is not part of the King's College Criteria. Liver failure is defined by loss of synthetic and metabolic function.
B.text: Very high ALT reflects the extent of hepatocellular necrosis but does not predict outcome and is not part of the King's College Criteria. Liver failure is defined by loss of synthetic and metabolic function.

C.html: Ingested dose guides initial risk assessment and NAC treatment but does not feature in transplant listing criteria, which depend on the biochemical and clinical severity of established failure.
C.text: Ingested dose guides initial risk assessment and NAC treatment but does not feature in transplant listing criteria, which depend on the biochemical and clinical severity of established failure.

D.html: Correct. An arterial pH < 7.30 after adequate fluid resuscitation independently satisfies the King's College Criteria for emergency liver transplantation in paracetamol-induced acute liver failure.
D.text: Correct. An arterial pH < 7.30 after adequate fluid resuscitation independently satisfies the King's College Criteria for emergency liver transplantation in paracetamol-induced acute liver failure.

q: A 42-year-old woman is referred with abnormal liver tests found during investigation of fatigue and pruritus. She is otherwise well. Investigations: ALP 410 U/L, ALT 52 U/L, bilirubin 18 µmol/L, IgM elevated. Anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) is positive at high titre. An ultrasound shows a normal biliary tree with no duct dilatation. She is diagnosed with a chronic cholestatic liver disease. Which single pharmacological treatment has been shown to improve biochemical markers and delay disease progression, and should be started first-line?
options: Prednisolone and azathioprine
Cholestyramine
Ursodeoxycholic acid
Rifampicin
Penicillamine
explain: High-titre AMA positivity, cholestatic LFTs (raised ALP), elevated IgM, pruritus and fatigue in a middle-aged woman with a normal biliary tree on imaging are diagnostic of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). 🫧 Pathologically there is autoimmune granulomatous destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts. First-line therapy is ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) 13–15 mg/kg/day. UDCA improves the biochemical profile (particularly ALP and bilirubin), delays histological progression and prolongs transplant-free survival. Response is assessed at 12 months (e.g. Paris/Toronto criteria); inadequate responders may receive obeticholic acid or bezafibrate as second-line. Cholestyramine and rifampicin treat cholestatic pruritus symptomatically but do not modify disease. Prednisolone/azathioprine is the treatment for autoimmune hepatitis (a hepatitic, not cholestatic, picture with raised transaminases and ASMA/anti-LKM). Penicillamine is used in Wilson's disease and has no role in PBC. Fat-soluble vitamin supplementation and bone protection (osteoporosis risk) are important adjuncts.

A.html: Corticosteroids with azathioprine are the treatment of autoimmune hepatitis, characterised by raised transaminases and ASMA/anti-LKM antibodies — a different picture from this cholestatic, AMA-positive presentation.

B.html: Cholestyramine is first-line for the pruritus of cholestasis but does not alter disease progression or biochemistry in PBC.
B.text: Cholestyramine is first-line for the pruritus of cholestasis but does not alter disease progression or biochemistry in PBC.

C.html: Correct. Ursodeoxycholic acid is first-line for PBC. It improves ALP and bilirubin, slows histological progression and prolongs transplant-free survival; response is assessed at 12 months.
C.text: Correct. Ursodeoxycholic acid is first-line for PBC. It improves ALP and bilirubin, slows histological progression and prolongs transplant-free survival; response is assessed at 12 months.

D.html: Rifampicin is a second-line agent for refractory cholestatic pruritus (via enzyme induction) but is not disease-modifying and carries hepatotoxicity risk requiring monitoring.

E.html: Penicillamine is a copper chelator used in Wilson's disease. Trials showed no benefit in PBC and it carries significant toxicity, so it has no role here.

q: A 24-year-old man is investigated for deranged liver tests and a 6-month history of tremor, dysarthria and deteriorating handwriting. His university tutor noted behavioural change. Examination shows a mild resting and intention tremor and hepatomegaly. Slit-lamp examination reveals golden-brown rings at the corneal margin. Investigations: ALT 96 U/L, low serum caeruloplasmin, 24-hour urinary copper markedly elevated. Which single mechanism best explains the accumulation of copper in this condition?
options: Increased intestinal absorption of dietary copper
Impaired hepatocyte biliary excretion of copper due to defective ATP7B transporter
Autoimmune destruction of copper-binding hepatocytes
Deficiency of the intestinal copper transporter ATP7A
Excess dietary copper intake overwhelming normal excretion
explain: This is Wilson's disease — a young adult with a movement disorder (tremor, dysarthria), neuropsychiatric change, hepatic involvement, Kayser–Fleischer rings, low caeruloplasmin and high urinary copper. 🧬 It is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in ATP7B, a hepatocyte copper-transporting ATPase. ATP7B has two roles: incorporating copper into apo-caeruloplasmin, and (critically) exporting excess copper into bile. When ATP7B is defective, copper cannot be excreted in bile and accumulates in hepatocytes, then spills into the circulation and deposits in the brain (basal ganglia), cornea (KF rings), kidneys and joints. Reduced copper incorporation into caeruloplasmin lowers serum caeruloplasmin, while free (non-caeruloplasmin-bound) copper rises and urinary copper increases. Intestinal absorption is normal — the defect is in biliary excretion, not uptake. ATP7A mutations cause Menkes disease (copper deficiency), the opposite phenotype. It is not autoimmune or dietary. Treatment is copper chelation with penicillamine or trientine, or zinc (blocks intestinal absorption).

ATP7B has two roles: incorporating copper into apo-caeruloplasmin, and (critically) exporting excess copper into bile. A.text: Intestinal copper absorption is essentially normal in Wilson's disease. The problem lies downstream in the hepatocyte's inability to excrete copper into bile.

B.html: Correct. Defective ATP7B impairs hepatocyte biliary copper excretion (and caeruloplasmin loading), so copper accumulates in the liver and spills over into brain, cornea and other tissues.
B.text: Correct. Defective ATP7B impairs hepatocyte biliary copper excretion (and caeruloplasmin loading), so copper accumulates in the liver and spills over into brain, cornea and other tissues.

C.html: Wilson's disease is a genetic transporter defect, not an autoimmune process. There is no autoimmune destruction of hepatocytes driving copper accumulation.
C.text: Wilson's disease is a genetic transporter defect, not an autoimmune process. There is no autoimmune destruction of hepatocytes driving copper accumulation.

D.html: ATP7A deficiency causes Menkes disease, an X-linked disorder of copper deficiency with kinky hair and neurodegeneration — the opposite of copper overload in Wilson's.
D.text: ATP7A deficiency causes Menkes disease, an X-linked disorder of copper deficiency with kinky hair and neurodegeneration — the opposite of copper overload in Wilson's.

E.html: Dietary copper intake is not excessive; the disease results from a genetic inability to excrete normal dietary copper via bile, leading to progressive accumulation.
E.text: Dietary copper intake is not excessive; the disease results from a genetic inability to excrete normal dietary copper via bile, leading to progressive accumulation.

q: A 61-year-old man presents to the emergency department with haematemesis and melaena. He has a history of alcohol-related cirrhosis. On arrival he is tachycardic at 118 bpm with a blood pressure of 94/58 mmHg. Investigations: haemoglobin 78 g/L, urea 14 mmol/L, platelets 88 x10^9/L. He is resuscitated with crystalloid and blood products, and started on terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics. He remains stable. According to BSG guidance, what is the most appropriate timing for upper GI endoscopy?
options: Immediately, before any resuscitation is undertaken
Within 24 hours of presentation, after resuscitation
Only if rebleeding occurs during admission
After 72 hours once liver function is optimised
As an outpatient within 2 weeks
explain: This is an acute upper GI bleed in a cirrhotic, most likely variceal haemorrhage. 🩸 Management priorities are resuscitation, terlipressin (splanchnic vasoconstriction, reduces portal pressure) and prophylactic antibiotics (reduce infection, rebleeding and mortality) — all started here. Per BSG/NICE (Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding) guidance, endoscopy should be performed within 24 hours of presentation after adequate resuscitation for all patients admitted with acute upper GI bleeding. For unstable patients with severe/ongoing bleeding, endoscopy should occur immediately after resuscitation. Variceal bleeding is treated with endoscopic band ligation (or sclerotherapy) at endoscopy. Endoscopy before resuscitation is unsafe — haemodynamic stabilisation comes first. Waiting for rebleeding, delaying to 72 hours, or arranging outpatient endoscopy would all be inappropriate and dangerous in an active bleed. If bleeding is uncontrolled, a Sengstaken–Blakemore/Minnesota tube can be used as a bridge to TIPS. This patient's raised urea with a GI bleed reflects absorbed blood protein and hypovolaemia.

Per BSG/NICE (Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding) guidance, endoscopy should be performed within 24 hours of presentation after adequate resuscitation for all patients admitted with acute upper GI bleeding. A.html: Endoscopy before resuscitation is unsafe; airway protection and haemodynamic stabilisation must come first. Sedation in an unresuscitated, actively bleeding patient risks aspiration and cardiovascular collapse.
A.text: Endoscopy before resuscitation is unsafe; airway protection and haemodynamic stabilisation must come first. Sedation in an unresuscitated, actively bleeding patient risks aspiration and cardiovascular collapse.

B.html: Correct. BSG/NICE recommend endoscopy within 24 hours of presentation after resuscitation for all acute upper GI bleeds, allowing diagnosis and endoscopic therapy such as variceal band ligation.

C.html: Waiting for rebleeding before endoscopy abandons the opportunity for early diagnosis and definitive endoscopic haemostasis, and worsens outcomes in variceal bleeding.
C.text: Waiting for rebleeding before endoscopy abandons the opportunity for early diagnosis and definitive endoscopic haemostasis, and worsens outcomes in variceal bleeding.

D.html: A 72-hour delay is unacceptable in acute variceal bleeding, where early band ligation reduces rebleeding and mortality. Liver function cannot be meaningfully 'optimised' before controlling the bleed.

q: A 30-year-old healthcare worker undergoes hepatitis B screening. Her results are: HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive at 240 mIU/mL, anti-HBc (total) negative, HBeAg negative, anti-HBe negative. She feels entirely well and has no risk factors. She asks what her results mean. Which single interpretation is correct?
options: Acute hepatitis B infection
Chronic hepatitis B infection with high infectivity
Past natural infection with resolution and immunity
Immunity due to previous hepatitis B vaccination
Occult hepatitis B infection
explain: The key to HBV serology is distinguishing vaccine-induced from natural immunity. 💉 This pattern — HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive, anti-HBc negative — indicates immunity from vaccination. Vaccines contain only surface antigen, so vaccinated individuals develop anti-HBs but never anti-HBc (which is generated only by exposure to the whole virus/core antigen during natural infection). Compare the alternatives: • Past natural infection (resolved): HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive, anti-HBc positive. The positive anti-HBc is the discriminator — absent here. • Acute infection: HBsAg positive, anti-HBc IgM positive. • Chronic infection: HBsAg positive >6 months, anti-HBc positive; HBeAg positive indicates high infectivity/replication. • Occult HBV: HBsAg negative but HBV DNA detectable, usually anti-HBc positive. Her anti-HBs of 240 mIU/mL confirms a protective response (>10 mIU/mL is protective). She is immune through vaccination and needs no further action beyond routine occupational-health follow-up.

Compare the alternatives: • Past natural infection (resolved): HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive, anti-HBc positive. The positive anti-HBc is the discriminator — absent here. • Acute infection: HBsAg positive, anti-HBc IgM positive. • Chronic infection: HBsAg positive >6 months, anti-HBc positive; HBeAg positive indicates high infectivity/replication. • Occult HBV: HBsAg negative but HBV DNA detectable, usually anti-HBc positive. Her anti-HBs of 240 mIU/mL confirms a protective response (>10 mIU/mL is protective). She is immune through vaccination and needs no further action beyond routine occupational-health follow-up.

B.html: Chronic infection requires persistent HBsAg positivity for over 6 months; HBeAg positivity would indicate high infectivity. This patient is HBsAg and HBeAg negative.

C.html: Resolved natural infection would show positive anti-HBc alongside positive anti-HBs. The negative anti-HBc here excludes prior natural infection and points to vaccination.

D.html: Correct. Isolated anti-HBs positivity with negative anti-HBc and HBsAg indicates vaccine-induced immunity, since the vaccine contains only surface antigen and never generates anti-core antibodies.

q: A 54-year-old man is admitted with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, vomiting and abdominal tenderness. He drinks 60 units of alcohol per week. Serum amylase is markedly elevated and CT confirms acute pancreatitis. On admission: age 54, white cell count 18 x10^9/L, glucose 12 mmol/L, urea 18 mmol/L, and albumin 28 g/L. At 48 hours: calcium 1.9 mmol/L, PaO2 7.5 kPa (on air), LDH 700 U/L, AST 250 U/L. Using the modified Glasgow (Imrie) score, how would you best classify the severity, and what does this indicate?
options: Score 1 — mild pancreatitis, ward-based care
Score 2 — mild pancreatitis, unlikely to need HDU
Score 3 — borderline, repeat scoring at 72 hours
Score 8 — but the Glasgow score does not predict severity
Score 7 — severe pancreatitis, predicting high risk of complications and mortality
explain: The modified Glasgow (Imrie) criteria use the mnemonic PANCREAS, each worth 1 point, assessed within 48 hours: 🧮 PaO₂ <8 kPa (7.5 ✓); Age >55 (54 ✗); Neutrophils/WCC >15 (18 ✓); Calcium <2 mmol/L (1.9 ✓); uRea >16 mmol/L (18 ✓); LDH >600 U/L or AST >200 (700 & 250 ✓ = 1 point); Albumin <32 g/L (28 ✓); Sugar (glucose) >10 mmol/L (12 ✓). That gives 7 points (age just misses at 54). A score ≥3 within 48 hours indicates severe/predicted-severe pancreatitis, warranting HDU/ITU-level care, aggressive fluid resuscitation and monitoring for complications (necrosis, organ failure, pseudocyst). A score of 7 predicts a high risk of complications and mortality. The other options miscount or wrongly dismiss the score. Alcohol and gallstones are the two commonest UK causes. The score does correlate with outcome — higher scores predict worse prognosis — so it is used precisely for risk stratification alongside CRP and clinical assessment.

B.html: A score of 2 also undercounts. With seven criteria satisfied the patient has predicted-severe pancreatitis and needs HDU/ITU-level care, not ward-only management.
